activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Gabriel ran to the playground. The sun was hot on his face. He wanted to go on the big slide. But the big slide was too hot to touch!

He looked around. There was a small slide in the shade. Gabriel touched it. It felt cold. "The sun made the big slide hot," he said. "No sun, so this one is cold." He patted the small slide with his towel. "You are my friend now."

Down he went, slow and easy. Then a big kid zipped by, fast like a bird. Gabriel laughed. "You are fast. I am slow. But I go again and again!"

After the slide, Gabriel found the water fountain. He pressed the button. Water went splash into his hands. The water was cold and he splashed his hot neck. He sat on his towel in the shade. It was quiet there. The tall tree made everything quiet and cool.

Then the clouds came. The sun went away. Gabriel touched the big slide again. It was cold now! "The sun went away, so now it is cold," he said. Up he climbed, one step, two steps, three.

Gabriel went down the big slide. He flew fast, fast, fast. "Sun makes it hot," he shouted. "No sun makes it cold. And me? I make it fun!" He ran to the ladder for one more turn.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Juliette loved the water. Every Saturday, her swim team came to the pool. Her team was called the Little Fish.

Juliette wore her float belt. The belt had soft foam blocks. The belt made her stay on top of the water. Without it, she sank down low. With it, she floated up high. She kicked her legs and moved like a fish.

One Saturday, Juliette wanted to jump off the tall step. She stood at the edge. She jumped in. The water went up in a big splash. Then the splash went away. She was floating. Her belt had kept her up. "The belt helps me float," she said.

Coach Maya smiled. "Good kicking, Juliette."

After swimming, the team sat on the towels. Mom had brought apples for a snack. Soon they would go home for dinner.

At the last swim day, everyone on the team got a ribbon. It was shiny and blue. Juliette held it tight. "I got this because I swam all season," she said.

Mom clapped. Juliette waved her ribbon at Coach Maya.

"I will be a Little Fish again next year," said Juliette.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Brooklyn stood at the bus stop with her grandpa. The wind blew. Her furry coat was in her bag. "Put it on, Brooklyn," said Grandpa. "It is cold."

Brooklyn pushed her arms in. One arm, two arms. Then she pulled the zipper. The zipper did not go up. She pulled again. It still did not go up. Grandpa waited. He hummed a little song. Brooklyn looked down. The two sides of the zipper were apart at the bottom. She pushed them together. Click. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. "It goes up because the bottom is together," said Brooklyn. "The bottom has to be together."

Grandpa smiled. "That's right," he said. He pulled a carrot from his bag. "A snack while we wait." Brooklyn munched her carrot. She zipped her coat down and up again, just to see it work. The bus came around the corner. Brooklyn held her furry sleeve up high and waved and waved.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Audrey had a cough. It kept her awake at night. Mom said, "We will call the pharmacist." The phone rang. The pharmacist had kind voice.

Mom took Audrey to the pharmacy. The pharmacist gave her a bottle and a small cup. "Use the cup," said Mom. "The cup has lines on it. The lines show how much." Audrey looked at the lines. One line was for little kids. She was a little kid.

At home, Mom poured up to the line. Audrey drank it. It tasted like cherry. Then Mom stacked two pillows and one more. The pillows made a triangle. Audrey leaned back on the triangle. Her cough got quiet. She could breathe easy.

"The cup and the pillows helped," said Audrey. Mom tucked the blanket under her chin. "Yes," said Mom. "Now close your eyes." Audrey held her bear tight. The lamp made a soft yellow circle on the wall. "Good night, Mom," she said.

story:

The sky was cloudy. A cool wind blew. Dad lit the candles. But the little flames went out. He lit them again. They went out again. The wind was blowing them out! Mia held up her hands. She made a wall with her palms. Dad lit one candle. It stayed lit. Then he lit them all. The flames stood still behind her hands.

"Sing now!" Mia called. Everyone sang Happy Birthday. Mia took a big breath. She blew and blew. Every candle went out at once. Grandma hugged her. "Make a wish," said Grandma. Dad went to lock the cake safe in the car. Sam woke up from his nap just in time for a big piece.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Dylan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He saw a little sink in the corner. A nurse stood by it and smiled.

"Wash your hands first," the nurse said. "Use soap and count to twenty." Dylan put his hands under the water. He rubbed the soap all over. "One, two, three," he counted. "Four, five, six." The bubbles grew big and white.

"How long is twenty?" Dylan asked. The nurse held up her fingers. "Count my fingers ten times, then you are done," she said. Dylan counted and counted. "Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" The bubbles went down the drain.

"Now my hands are clean!" said Dylan. He looked at them shine. "Germs go down the drain because I washed them off," he said. "I will wash before I eat too. And after the potty!" The nurse clapped her hands. Dylan waved his clean hands like flags. "Look at me, whole world!" he shouted. "My hands are soap clean!"

story:
It was a rainy day. Big drops hit the window. Asher held Mommy's hand at the store.

"Rain makes the window wet," Asher said.

The store did not sell toys. It sold paint and paper. A craft table stood by the door. Asher sat down to paint a frog. But there was no green paint. Only red, blue, and yellow cups.

Asher felt worried. "My frog needs green," he said.

Mommy smiled. "Try mixing two colors," she said.

Asher dipped his brush in yellow. He painted a stripe. Then he dipped in blue. He touched the yellow stripe. The paint turned green on the paper!

"Yellow and blue make green!" Asher said.

He painted one big green frog. Then he drew red lips and a blue hat on it. The rain went tap, tap, tap on the roof. Asher and Mommy walked home with the dry frog picture held up high.

story:
Romy wanted her teddy bear. He sat on the high shelf. She was too small to reach him.

Romy looked around the playroom. The big chair was tall. The small chair was short. She pushed the big chair to the shelf. She climbed up. Still too short! Then she saw the big red block. She put the block on the chair. She climbed again. Her hand touched teddy's soft foot. She pulled him down.

"Got you!" she said.

Then the block began to slide. "Fast!" said Romy. The chair tipped over. The block fell. Bump! It hit the floor. Romy sat down and pouted. She was mad at the chair.

Her brother Ben ran in. "Was that you?" he asked.

"The block fell fast because it was big and heavy," Romy said. "Small things fall slow."

Ben picked up a tiny block. He let it drop. It fell slow and soft. Then he dropped the big block. It fell fast and hard. Bump again!

"See?" said Ben. "You taught me that!" said Romy.

Just then teddy's hat slipped off. Under it was a sign. It said "Kiss me here." Romy laughed. She kissed teddy on his soft head. Teddies don't get too hot or too cold, she thought. They are just right.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Naomi stood in the reading corner. She saw big books and little books. One book had a bear on the cover. The bear wore a red hat.

A librarian came over. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Naomi nodded. She got a new card with her name on it. The letters made her smile.

She took the bear book to the desk. "I want to keep this forever," Naomi said. The librarian smiled. "You can take it home," she said. "But other kids want to read it too. So you bring it back soon."

Naomi held the book tight. She tried to think. If she kept it, other kids could not read about the bear. That made her feel sad for them.

"Okay," she said. "I will bring it back." She drew a circle around the day on the paper. That was the day the book went back.

At home, Naomi read the bear book three times. Then she put it by the door. "I will see you again," she told the bear.

story:
Layla wanted to help Mom cook. She saw a big pot on the stove. "Can I stir?" she asked. Mom said, "Not yet. Wait for the soup." So Layla waited.

Mom gave her a small gift. It was an orange in a heavy bag. Layla touched it with her fingers. It felt bumpy. She smelled it with her nose. It smelled sweet. She heard the soup bubble. Her ears told her it was hot. "It talks!" said Layla, and she laughed.

Mom cut the orange. Layla tasted it with her tongue. "Sour and sweet!" she said. Then Mom let her stir. The spoon was too big, so her arm went slow. She tried again. The soup turned round and round. "My eyes saw it spin!" said Layla. "Because I stirred it." Mom kissed her head. "Good little cook," said Mom.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's farm today. Yesterday, Grandma had called. "The brown egg is warm," Grandma said. "A chick will come out soon."

"Is it now?" Paisley asked. "Not now," said Mom. "We drive now. We get there later." Paisley looked out the window. A wild bird flew by. "That bird can fly now," she said. "I want to fly now too." Mom smiled. "Later, little one. First we drive."

The car went slow, then fast, then slow again. Paisley counted the cows. One, two, three. Then the car stopped. "We are here now!" said Mom.

Paisley ran to the coop. She looked at the brown egg. It was shaking. Tap, tap, tap. A small hole appeared. Then a wet little chick popped out. "It came out!" Paisley said. She thought hard. "The egg sat and sat. Then the chick came out. It took a long, long time." Grandma nodded. "Now you learn how chicks come," she said. Paisley touched the soft chick with one finger. "Hello, chick. You hatched today." Just then, the second egg began to tap too.

story:
Audrey wanted the big red truck. Ben had it. Ben pushed the truck round and round the rug. It made a loud brmm sound. Audrey waited. She counted to ten. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Ben still did not stop.

Audrey grabbed the truck. The truck tipped over. Blocks went crash. A cup of water began to spill. Ben shouted, "My truck!" Audrey felt her face go hot. Dad came over on slow feet. He knelt down by the rug.

"Dad, I want a turn," said Audrey. "Then use your name and ask," said Dad. Audrey took a big breath. "Ben, can I have a turn, please?" Ben looked at the truck. Then he looked at Audrey. "Okay. When I get to the door," said Ben.

Ben pushed the truck to the toy door. Then he gave it to Audrey. Audrey pushed it to the door too. "Your turn," she said. Ben smiled. Dad said, "Look at that. Asking works." Ben gave Audrey the cup. Audrey drank her water. It was not spilled after all.

They took turns, one, two, one, two. The truck went back and forth all morning. Dad sat close by the blocks. The playroom was warm and sunny. "Best truck day ever," said Ben. "Best truck day ever," said Audrey.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Charlie was at soccer practice. There was one big yellow ball. Max wanted to kick it too.

Charlie grabbed the ball and ran. Max grabbed it back. Then the ball popped right out of both hands. It rolled under the bench. Nobody got to kick it.

Coach Zoe blew her whistle. "One ball, two friends," she said. "Take turns."

Charlie thought hard. He had an idea. "You go first," he said to Max. Max kicked the ball to the goal. Then Max sent it back with his foot. "Your turn, star player!" said Max.

Charlie ran and kicked the ball high. It went over the goal and landed in Coach Zoe's hat. Everyone laughed. "Oops," said Charlie.

The coach shook the ball out of her hat. "Good kick," she said. "See what happens? When you wait, the ball comes back to you."

Charlie nodded. "Grabbing made it roll away," he said. "Waiting sends it back!"

At the end, the team played a friendly little game. Max and Charlie shared the ball the whole time. "Best kick team ever," said Max.

Charlie smiled and kicked the ball one more time.

story:
Lily stood in the big kitchen. The cook, Ben, gave her warm toast. "Be my helper," he said. Lily wanted to butter the toast all by herself.

She pushed the butter with her knife. It slid around. Then Lily saw the toast was warm. The warm toast made the butter soft. The soft butter spread easy. "Look!" said Lily. "I made a butter map on my toast!" Ben smiled. The butter covered every bit.

Next came the milk. Lily held the cup. She poured from way up high. Milk splashed out. "Oh no," said Lily. So she held the cup close to the jug. She tipped it slow. The milk went in quiet. Not one drop fell. "I did it!" said Lily. Ben clapped. "Here is your milk, and here is mine," said Lily, handing him a cup.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Ella went to the pet store with Dad. She saw a little orange fish. "I want that one," she said. The man put the fish in a bag of water. Dad helped Ella carry it. The bag felt heavy but she was strong.

At home, they put the fish in a small tank. Ella wanted to feed him. She tipped the food jar. Lots of flakes fell in. "So many!" she said.

The next morning the water was cloudy. Ella could not see her fish. Dad said, "Try one little pinch." Ella picked up two flakes. She dropped them in. The fish ate them fast.

Day by day the water got clear again. "Too much food made the water cloudy," Ella said. "Little bit for the little fish." Every morning she gave one small pinch. The fish swam round and round, and his tail went swish.

story:
Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her cup was empty. She wanted more milk.

"More," she said. Papa kept cutting his bread. "More," she said again. Papa still did not move.

Then Mama said, "Papa, please pass the bread." Papa passed the bread right away. Sienna watched with wide eyes.

She waited for her turn. "Papa, please may I have milk?" she asked. Papa got up and poured the milk. "Thank you," said Sienna. Papa smiled a big smile.

Sienna took a sip. She reached for the bread and bumped her spoon. Clang! Peas rolled under the table. One pea, two peas, three little peas.

"Sorry, Mama," said Sienna. "I bumped my spoon." Mama said, "You can ask for help." Sienna waited while Mama picked up one pea, two peas, three little peas.

After dinner, Papa said, "Want to go to the playground?" Sienna slid down the big slide, one time, two times, three times.

"Thank you, Papa," she said. "That was because I said please."

story:
Camille sat down for dinner. Papa put one big corn bread on the table. Camille wanted the first big piece.

"I will cut it," said Papa. "Then we each take one piece." He cut the bread into four pieces. One piece was big. One piece was small. Camille grabbed the big piece fast.

Mama looked at her plate. "My piece is small," said Mama. Camille looked around the table. Papa had a small piece too. Baby Sam had crumbs.

"Wait," said Camille. "If I take the big one, you get the small ones." She put the big piece back on the plate. She pushed it to Mama. Then she took a middle piece for herself.

Just then a bug flew in the window. It landed near the bread. "Go away, bug!" said Camille. "That is our food." Papa carried the bug outside on a napkin.

"Dinner has a rule," said Camille. "We all get the same size, so it is fair." Then she smelled something. "Papa, your shoes are smelly!" Everyone laughed. Sam laughed too.

"Papa, wash your feet," said Camille. "Then come back for bread."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Bennett woke up in his bedroom. The sun was not there. Rain tapped on his round window. Tap, tap, tap.

Bennett wanted his swing. "Can I swing now?" he asked. "Not now," said Grandma. "The rain makes the swing wet. You can swing tomorrow." Bennett looked out. The swing hung by the tree. Rain dripped off the seat. Drip, drip, drip.

Bennett remembered yesterday. Yesterday the sun was out. Yesterday the swing was dry. Yesterday he went up so high. "Yesterday I swung and swung," he said. "But yesterday is all done." He missed his swing. He wanted it now.

So Bennett found his round red ball. He rolled it on the floor. He rolled it under the bed. "Later I will get my ball," he said. "Later, after my nap." He yawned a big yawn.

Grandma tucked him in. "Sleep now," she said. "Then tomorrow comes. Tomorrow the rain stops. Tomorrow the sun comes out." Bennett smiled. "Then the swing dries," he said. "Then I swing and swing." His eyes closed. The rain tapped soft. Tap, tap, tap.

story:
Grandpa came on the big red bus. He would stay for seven whole days. Ali counted on his fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

Grandpa liked to make pancakes in the morning. But Grandpa could not find his glasses. "Oh dear," he said. He looked in his bag. He looked under the table.

Ali wanted to help. He let Grandpa sit down. Then Ali looked in the kitchen. He saw something shiny in the pan cupboard. It was the glasses! Grandpa had put them there when he hid the chocolate.

"You sat on them?" asked Ali. "No, I hid sweets there," laughed Grandpa. "Then I lost my glasses too!" Ali laughed too. He put the glasses on Grandpa's nose.

"You found them because you are small," said Grandpa. "You can see down low." Ali felt very proud. He helped make the pancakes. He helped keep the kitchen tidy. Every morning after that, Ali looked in the cupboard first.

"Any more chocolate?" he asked. Grandpa winked. "Look in my shoe," he said.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Clara rides in the car to the field. Her team wears blue shirts. Today is her first real game.

Clara stands by the tee. The ball sits on the tee. She holds the bat with two hands. She swings. She misses. The team is quiet. She waits. She swings again. The ball goes pop and rolls in the grass.

Clara holds the bat tight. She runs with it. The bat is heavy. Her feet go slow. The coach calls, "Drop the bat, Clara!" Clara lets go of the bat. Her hands are free. Now her feet go fast. She runs to the base. She steps on it with one foot.

"You made it," says her friend Ben. Clara looks back. The bat lies in the dirt. She sees why her feet were slow. "The bat made me slow," she says. "My feet are fast with no bat."

The next batter hits the ball. Clara claps from the base. The sun feels warm on her head.

At home, Clara puts her bat by her bed. She pats it once. "Night, night, bat," she says.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Luka went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about trucks. Luka felt excited. His tummy jumped like a grasshopper.

He ran to the truck shelf. The truck book was gone! Luka felt angry. He stomped his foot. Then he felt sad. A big tear rolled down his cheek.

A girl named Mia saw him. "This book fell behind the shelf," she said. Luka peeked. There it was! A loud thump had made the book fall, because the shelf was wobbly. Luka picked it up. He was scared of the dark gap, but Mia held his hand. Luka smiled. "Happy again," he said. At home, he asked for water and a sweet apple. Mom read the truck book twice. "I love the library," Luka said.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Sienna ran into the community centre. It was stormy outside, so playtime was inside today. On the table sat two bowls of crackers.

"I want the one with more!" said Sienna.

She counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." Then the second. "One, two, three." Five is more than three!

Tom counted her bowl from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five," he said.

"You got five too!" Sienna cried. "I counted from that side. You counted from this side. We still got five!"

She ate a cracker. "Five!" she said, holding up fingers. "I have five crackers, because five was my last number!"

Outside, the stormy sky rumbled. Inside, Sienna munched and grinned.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Parker stood at the edge of the backyard pool. His green swim ring sat in the water. It went up and down on the little waves. "I want to swim like a fish," said Parker. Dad put water wings on his arms. "Now kick," said Dad.

Parker jumped in with a splash. His arms floated up all by themselves. "My arms go up!" said Parker. He kicked his legs. He did not sink. He moved like a little boat. Dad clapped and cheered.

Then Dad took the water wings off. Parker held Dad's hand. His arms went down in the water. "No wings, no float," said Parker. "Wings make me float." Dad smiled. "We will practice more after lunch." Parker chased a leaf across the shallow end. "Look at me," he said. "I swim."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Emily wanted warm milk before bed. The milk in the fridge felt cold. "So cold," she said, and shivered.

Mom poured the milk into a pot. The pot sat on the hot stove. Emily watched. Big bubbles came up in the small pot. The milk went fast, fast, fast. Then Mom turned the knob. Now the bubbles went slow, slow, slow.

"Why did it get slow?" Emily asked. She looked at the knob. Mom had made the stove less hot. "Less hot makes it slow," Emily said. "Is that true?" Mom smiled and nodded.

Emily held her cup. The milk was warm now. She took a tiny sip. Then a big sip.

"Can milk swim in my tummy?" she asked.

Mom laughed, and poured a little more.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Milo went to the farmers' market with Grandpa. He saw big red tomatoes on a stand. "I want to grow one," said Milo. A farmer gave him a tiny seed. "Seeds need water every day," Grandpa said.

Milo planted the seed near the fence. He gave it water on Monday. On Tuesday he forgot. On Wednesday he forgot again. The pot looked dry. Nothing grew.

Milo was sad. "My seed is broken," he said. Grandpa knelt down by him. "The seed is dry. Dry seeds sleep. Let's water it together." Milo gave the seed a big drink of water. He watered it every day after that.

Soon a little green sprout popped up. A bird flew by with twigs for its nest. Milo clapped his hands. "Water made it grow!" he said. Grandpa smiled and gave him a hug.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Hunter ran to the playground after school. He looked in his cubby. His little blue dinosaur was not there. "Where did you go, Dino?" he asked. His heart felt heavy.

"I must find him," Hunter said. He thought hard. "Where did I play last?" He had played on the slide first. He looked under the slide. Only sand was there.

Then he had played in the grass. He had pretended the grass was a jungle. He walked to the jungle spot. He looked down. There was Dino, lying in the green grass!

"You were in the jungle the whole time," Hunter said. "I found you because I walked my steps again." He hugged Dino close.

His teacher smiled. "Time to go home, Hunter," she said.

"Okay," Hunter said. He held Dino tight. He was polite and said, "Thank you for waiting, Teacher." Then he waved goodbye to the slide, and to the grass. "Bye, jungle," he whispered to Dino. "Let's go home."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Connor was a little kid on a big trip. His family had a hotel room. Connor put his brown teddy on the bed. "We are home now, teddy," he said.

But then the lights went out. The room went dark. "Mom! Mom!" Connor began to yell. Mom came fast. "I am here," she said.

Dad held a little card. "Watch this," he said. He put the card in the slot by the door. Click. The lights came on. Dad took the card out. Click. The lights went off. Connor laughed. "The card makes the lights!" he said.

Connor tried it himself. Card in, lights on. Card out, lights off. "I can do it," he said. Then he saw teddy in the dark corner. Connor put the card in the slot. The lights came on. Ted was safe. Connor hugged him tight.

At night, Dad took the card to the desk. "Sleep now," said Mom. The room got dark and soft. Connor held teddy close. "The card is sleeping too," he whispered. Ted's brown ear touched Connor's nose.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Aiden sat on Grandpa's big couch. The room was loud and warm. One team, two teams, lots of fans. Grandma painted a little red star on his finger. "There," she said. "Now you are a fan too." Grandpa blew a long, sharp whistle with his mouth when the game started.

Then everyone yelled, "Go, go, go!" They all stood up. They jumped. They waved their arms. Aiden could not see the TV. He saw backs and elbows and a big hat. "I can't see!" he said. His cousin Mia heard him. She pulled a small chair to the front. "Sit here," she said. Aiden climbed up. Now he was tall.

Just then his team scored. Aiden missed it. He missed the ball and the net and everything. His lip went down. Grandpa sat next to him. "Watch now," said Grandpa. "The TV will show it again." Aiden watched. One, two, three seconds went by. Then the ball came back on the screen. It flew and flew and went in! "Again!" said Aiden. "The TV shows it again!" Everyone laughed and jumped one more time. "Again, again!" said Aiden.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Hayden went to the pharmacy with his dad. His nose was runny and red. Dad got a small box of tissues. Then Hayden saw a little bottle of soap next to the tissues. It smelled like honey. He wanted it.

At home, Dad said it was time to eat. "First we wash," said Dad. Hayden let the water rain down on his hands. He rubbed the honey soap all over. His shadow sat small on the floor by the sink. Dad counted, "One, two, three." Hayden counted too. They counted all the way to twenty. The soap bubbles went pop, pop, pop.

Then Hayden ate his sandwich. His hands were clean. "No germs on my bread," he said. "Twenty seconds did it." Dad smiled and gave him one more bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Jo held up her hands. "We will clap and sing today," she said. The song was "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star."

Eva wanted to sing it all by herself. But her claps went too fast. Her claps ran ahead of the song. Then the words fell out of her mouth. She stopped and frowned.

Miss Jo clapped once. "Twinkle," she sang. She clapped again. "Twinkle," she sang. Eva watched. One clap came with one word. Not two claps. Just one.

Eva tried it. She clapped on "Twin" and skipped to "kle." The clap went in the middle of the word. That was the trick!

"Does one clap help?" Eva asked herself. "Yes. One clap for each big word."

The whole class clapped together now. Clap, word, clap, word. It was a huge sound, like soft rain on the roof.

Eva sang the rhyme from memory. She did not miss one word. She clapped on the beat all the way to "what you are."

Miss Jo smiled at Eva. "That was a big number of claps," she said.

"Twinkle, twinkle," Eva sang again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He wanted to paint a green frog. Green was his favorite color. But Grandma had no green paint.

"Look in the basket," said Grandma. Weston found red, blue, and yellow. He saw a puzzle on the table too. A frog puzzle! The frog on the box was big and green.

Weston looked hard at his paints. No green anywhere. He dipped his brush in blue. He made a blue stripe. Then he dipped in yellow. He mixed them on the paper with his brush. Round and round went his wrist.

"Grandma! Look!" The blue and yellow made green! "Blue and yellow make green," said Weston. Grandma clapped her hands.

Weston painted his frog green. Then Grandma brought red juice with ice. The ice began to melt in the sun. Weston laughed and painted a red sun too. "My frog has a sunny day!"
